title: Step-size trace vs stability ceiling: is the adaptive solver limited by accuracy or stability?
summary: For stiff problems an adaptive solver's step size is often set by stability, not by accuracy. This trace puts the accepted step h(t) beside a ceiling computed from the fastest eigenvalue, so you can see which of the two is in charge at each moment.

media.alt: Log-log plot of accepted step size against time, riding a dashed stability ceiling from about 7e-4 up to about 0.28, with a small shaded stability-limited region.
media.caption: Reference render of class F5.4 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: Is the adaptive solver limited by accuracy or stability?
read_the_figure.axes: x: time t in seconds, logarithmic (1e-4 to 10). y: step size h in seconds, logarithmic (about 2e-4 to 0.3).
look_at: Where does the accepted step touch the ceiling, and for how long (how many decades of time)?
Where is it clearly below the ceiling? There the step is limited by accuracy or by the controller ramping up.
How far does the ceiling rise as the fastest transient dies out?
Is the ceiling computed from the current eigenvalue, and is the formula stated?
as_drawn: The dashed ceiling is 2.78 / |lambda_max(t)|, with |lambda_max| falling from about 4000 to 10 as a fast mode decays. It rises from about 7e-4 s to about 0.28 s, a factor of about 400.
The accepted step starts near 2.5e-4 s, climbs and sits on the ceiling from about 1e-3 s to about 2 s, then falls clearly below it (about 0.06 to 0.13 s) at late times.
The rose fill marks the stability-limited region, but it is very thin because the step hugs the ceiling; the annotation in the upper left states the conclusion in words.
Both axes are logarithmic, so a vertical gap is a ratio, not a difference.
read_the_figure.proves: If the accepted step rides the ceiling while the problem is smooth, accuracy is not the bottleneck: the solver is paying for stability, and an implicit or stabilised method could take far larger steps. It is a diagnosis, not a proof of the method's quality.
if_wrong: Step well below the ceiling throughout: the solver is accuracy-limited, so tightening the tolerance or a higher-order method is the lever, not stiffness.
Step above the ceiling: the ceiling is for the wrong method or the wrong eigenvalue, or the problem is nonlinear and the Jacobian changed.
No stated constant: the ceiling constant depends on the method (2.78 here is RK4's real-axis limit).
must_check: ceiling line: without it you cannot tell a step limited by stability from one limited by accuracy.
log axis: the step and the ceiling change by orders of magnitude, so a linear axis would flatten the stiff period.

terms.meaning: A solver that chooses h(t) from an error estimate, small where the solution changes quickly.
The largest step the method can take without the fastest eigenvalue leaving the stability region: the real-axis limit divided by |lambda_max|.
A problem with widely separated time scales: a fast mode dies out quickly but still constrains an explicit method's step.
The step is kept at the ceiling by stability, not by the accuracy requirement.
The step is set by the local error estimate and sits below the ceiling.

remember: Ceiling = real-axis limit / |lambda_max|; for RK4 the constant is about 2.785.
Step on the ceiling means stability is limiting.
Step below the ceiling means accuracy is limiting.
The ceiling moves as the Jacobian's eigenvalues move.
A stiff solver pays for the fast mode long after it has died.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Position on x is time, position on y is step size, both logarithmic. The solid teal line is what the solver actually did; the dashed amber line is the largest step it could safely have taken; the rose fill between them is drawn only where the step rides the ceiling. Two lines of different style and colour keep the plot readable in greyscale.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: Plain language: an explicit method has a speed limit set by the fastest decaying mode. If the solver keeps hitting that speed limit, it is stability that slows it down. Drawing the limit next to the actual speed turns this into a gap you can see. A log axis shows both the early period, where h is tiny, and the late period, where h is hundreds of times larger.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: The ceiling uses one number (the largest eigenvalue magnitude), so complex eigenvalues near the imaginary axis can be limited by a different part of the region. If the problem is nonlinear, the Jacobian eigenvalue changes with the state and must be re-evaluated. A step that rides the ceiling by design of the controller, as in the first decade here, can look stability-limited when it is merely the controller ramping up.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: The F5.2 stability-region plot explains where the constant comes from. The F6.1 eigenvalue-versus-time plot shows the stiffness itself. A work-precision diagram (F5.9) compares explicit and implicit solvers on cost instead of on a single trace.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add a second panel below sharing the time axis with the largest eigenvalue magnitude, shade stability-limited intervals only, and draw the same trace for an implicit solver as a third line to show how far it rises above the explicit ceiling.

steps.title: The ceiling from the stability region
steps.note: The constant is the real-axis limit from F5.2. For explicit Euler it would be 2.

steps.title: Ceiling ratio from the eigenvalue ratio
steps.note: In the render |lambda_max| falls from about 4010 to 10, so the ceiling rises about 400 times.

steps.title: Steps spent while stability-limited
steps.note: A long stiff stretch costs many steps even though the solution is smooth.

worked.title: Reading the stability ceiling from the reference render
worked.problem: Using the figure: (1) What are the ceiling values at t = 1e-4 s and at t = 10 s, and how many times larger is the second? (2) Which eigenvalue magnitudes do those correspond to? (3) Roughly how many steps does the solver spend between t = 1e-3 s and t = 0.1 s?

solution.text: (1) Read the dashed line: about 7e-4 s at the left and about 0.28 s at the right.
(2) Invert the ceiling formula with c = 2.78.
So the fast mode dominates early (4000 per second) and the slow mode (10 per second) remains.
(3) Over that stretch the step sits at about 7e-4 to 8.5e-4 s, so the number of steps is the elapsed time over the step.

worked.answer: The ceiling rises about 400-fold, from |lambda_max| of about 4000 to about 10; about 130 steps are spent in the first tenth of a second purely to keep the fast mode stable, even though the solution is smooth there.

analyze.q: At late times the step falls below the ceiling. What now sets it?
analyze.hint: Compare to the F6.5-style idea of an error estimate.

analyze.q: If an implicit method replaced the solver, where would its step sit relative to the ceiling, and why?
analyze.hint: Its stability region includes the left half-plane.

analyze.q: Why is it misleading to read the step trace without knowing how the solver ramps its first step?
analyze.hint: Look at the first decade of time.

evaluate.q: A user concludes that the method is unstable at t < 1e-3 because h is far below the ceiling there. Do you agree?
evaluate.hint: What does being below the ceiling mean?

create: Plot the same ceiling for explicit Euler (constant 2) and RK4 (constant 2.785) and mark the factor between them.
Add a third curve for a solver with a smaller tolerance and show where it becomes accuracy-limited.

checks.q: What does it mean when the accepted step lies on the ceiling?
checks.hint: Which of the two constraints is binding?
checks.answer: That stability, not accuracy, is limiting the step: a larger step would put the fastest eigenvalue outside the stability region.

checks.q: |lambda_max| = 500 per second and the method is RK4. What is the ceiling?
The step is far below the ceiling for the whole run. What lever helps and which does not?
checks.answer: The run is accuracy-limited: relax the tolerance or use a higher-order method. An implicit stiff solver would not help because stability is not the constraint.
